### Pollards Yard FAQs

Which homes at Pollards Yard are available to rent?
We are letting seven brand-new homes on plots 16 to 22: five two bedroom Polden homes on plots 16 to 20 and two four bedroom Loxleigh homes on plots 21 and 22. They will be available to rent soon.
Where is Pollards Yard?
Pollards Yard is a new development off Monmouth Street in the centre of Bridgwater, Somerset. It is opposite Bridgwater bus station, where the Hinkley Point C buses pick up, about a 10 minute walk from Bridgwater railway station and a short walk from the town centre shops and supermarkets.
How much is the rent?
Rents are available on request. Register your interest or call us on 01823 765654 and we will send you the rent, availability and viewing times.
Do the homes have electric vehicle charging?
Yes. Every home has its own electric vehicle charging point, and broadband is ready from the first day.
How are the homes heated?
Each home has Dimplex Wi-Fi electric radiators you can control from your phone and a Dimplex heat pump hot water cylinder that heats water using energy from the outside air. Windows and doors are A-rated double glazed, and many homes have solar panels.
How do I arrange a viewing?
Fill in the register your interest form on this page or call Quantock Lettings on 01823 765654. We will be in touch with viewing times as soon as the homes are ready.

## Privacy notice
URL: https://quantocklettings.co.uk/privacy

This notice explains how Quantock Lettings Ltd collects, uses and protects personal information when you use this website or get in touch with us. Last updated 30 October 2026.

### Who we are

Quantock Lettings Ltd is the data controller for the personal information described here. We are a company registered in England and Wales, company number 15929562, based at 1 The Crescent, Taunton TA1 4EA.

If you have any questions about this notice or your information, email our office or call 01823 765654.

### What we collect

When you fill in a form on this website, we collect the details you give us. These are your name, email address, phone number, preferred method of contact, your message and, for landlords, details of your property such as its address, postcode, type and number of bedrooms. The form also tells us which page it was sent from and how you reached the website.

When you email or phone us, we keep a record of what you tell us so that we can help you.

### How we use it

- To reply to your enquiry, arrange a rental valuation or viewing, and talk to you about our services.
- To take the steps you ask for before entering into an agreement with us, such as moving the management of your property to us.
- To keep a record of our dealings with you and meet our legal obligations.

We use your information because it is necessary to respond to your request and in our legitimate interest to run our lettings business. We do not use it for marketing unless you ask us to, and we never sell it.

If you become a landlord or tenant with us, we will give you separate information about how we handle your details as part of the tenancy, including referencing, right to rent checks and deposit protection.

### Who we share it with

- Formspree, which delivers the website forms to our inbox. Formspree is based in the United States, and transfers are made under appropriate safeguards required by UK data protection law.
- Microsoft, which provides our email.
- Our professional advisers, or regulators and authorities where the law requires it.

### How long we keep it

We keep enquiries for as long as we need them to deal with your request. If you do not go on to use our services, we delete them within two years. If you do, we keep your records for as long as the law requires.

### Cookies and this website

This website does not use advertising or analytics cookies. If you save a home using the heart button, that list is stored only in your own browser. Some photographs are loaded from Unsplash, which receives the technical details any website receives when it supplies an image, such as your IP address.

### Your rights

You have the right to ask for a copy of your information, to have it corrected or deleted, to object to or restrict how we use it, and to have it transferred. To make a request, contact us using the details above. We will respond within one month.

If you are unhappy with how we have handled your information, please tell us first so we can put it right. You can also complain to the Information Commissioner's Office at ico.org.uk or on 0303 123 1113.

Landlord guide · 2026 edition

## Letting your home,
made simple.

A plain-English guide for landlords in Taunton and the Quantocks: getting ready to let, the rules that apply in 2026, and how we look after you and your tenants.

01823 765654

Contact form: https://quantocklettings.co.uk/#contact

Updated for the Renters' Rights Act

Welcome
Welcome

### Thank you for thinking of us

Letting a home is a big decision, whether it's your first property or one of many. This guide explains what's involved, what the law expects of you in 2026, and how we can take as much or as little of the work off your hands as you'd like.

We're a small, local team based in Taunton. We let and manage homes across Taunton, Bridgwater, Wellington, Bishops Lydeard and the Quantock villages, and we live and work in the same communities as the landlords and tenants we look after.

Our approach is simple. We're honest about what your property will let for, we take time to find the right tenant rather than the first one, and we keep you informed without drowning you in paperwork. When something needs doing, you'll speak to someone who knows your property by name.

Renting has changed a great deal this year. The Renters' Rights Act came into force on 1 May 2026, and more changes follow in 2027 and beyond. We've written this guide so you can see exactly where you stand. If anything isn't clear, just call us.

Neil, Cheryl and Hattie

Before you let
Before you let

### Getting your property ready

A little preparation goes a long way. Homes that are clean, safe and well presented let faster, attract better tenants and tend to stay let for longer.

#### Permissions to check first

- Mortgage lender. If the property has a residential mortgage, you'll usually need your lender's consent before letting it.
- Freeholder or management company. If the property is leasehold, check the lease allows letting and whether you need to tell anyone.
- Insurance. Standard home insurance rarely covers a let property. Tell your insurer you're letting and make sure the cover is suitable for a rented home.
- Joint owners. Everyone named on the title should agree to the let.

#### Furnished or unfurnished?

Most homes in our area let unfurnished, often with white goods and floor coverings included. If you do provide furniture, it must meet fire safety rules, and it's worth keeping everything simple, sturdy and easy to replace.

#### What will it let for?

We'll visit, look at the property properly and give you an honest figure based on what similar homes are actually letting for locally. Pricing correctly from the start is the single biggest factor in letting quickly. Under the new rules we must advertise a clear asking rent and can't invite bids above it, so getting the figure right matters more than ever.

##### Presentation checklist

- Deep clean throughout, including carpets, oven and windows
- Fresh, neutral paint where walls are marked
- Garden tidy, hedges cut, paths clear
- Repairs done: dripping taps, sticking doors, loose fittings
- All appliances working, with manuals left in the property
- Any signs of damp or mould dealt with at the source
- Personal belongings, loft and shed contents removed
- A full set of keys for each tenant, plus one for us

Your legal responsibilities
Your legal responsibilities

### Safety and legal checklist

The main legal requirements for letting a home in England. We can arrange all of them, and on our fully managed service we track every renewal date for you.

Requirement | What the law expects

Gas safety certificate Every 12 months | All gas appliances, pipes and flues checked by a Gas Safe registered engineer. Tenants get a copy before moving in and within 28 days of each check.

Electrical safety report (EICR) At least every 5 years | Fixed wiring inspected by a qualified electrician, with urgent faults fixed within 28 days. Tenants get a copy before moving in.

Energy Performance Certificate Valid for 10 years | Shown in adverts and given to tenants. The property must currently be rated E or above, and the government plans to raise this to C by 2030.

Smoke and CO alarms Tested at every new tenancy | A smoke alarm on every storey used as living space, and a carbon monoxide alarm in any room with a fixed fuel-burning appliance (except gas cookers). Repair promptly when reported.

Legionella risk assessment Reviewed regularly | Assess the risk from the water system and take simple steps to control it.

Furniture and furnishings When furnishing | Upholstered furniture you supply must meet fire safety standards and carry the correct labels.

Right to Rent Before every tenancy | Check every adult tenant has the right to rent in the UK, and keep copies of the evidence.

Deposit protection Within 30 days | Protect the deposit in a government-approved scheme and give the tenant the prescribed information. Deposits are capped at five weeks' rent (six if the annual rent is £50,000 or more).

A safe, decent home Ongoing | Free of serious hazards such as damp and mould, with the structure, heating and hot water kept in good repair.

Licensing Usually every 5 years | Homes shared by five or more people from two or more households need an HMO licence. We check Somerset Council's current rules for your property.

Landlord registration New, renewed yearly | Landlords must register themselves and each let property on the new government database. See page 6.

Why it matters. Councils can fine landlords up to £7,000 for many breaches, and up to £40,000 for serious or repeated ones. Tenants can also apply to get rent back, and missing paperwork can stop you regaining possession.

Renting in 2026
Renting in 2026

### The Renters' Rights Act, in plain English

The biggest change to renting in England for over 30 years took effect on 1 May 2026. It applies to every private tenancy, including ones that started before that date. Here's what it means for you.

#### What changed on 1 May 2026

- No more fixed terms. All tenancies now roll from month to month. Tenants can leave at any time by giving two months' notice.
- Section 21 has gone. "No-fault" evictions have ended. To regain possession you must use a Section 8 notice and a specific legal reason, such as selling, moving in, or rent arrears. See page 10.
- Rent reviews once a year. Rent can only go up once a year, using a formal Section 13 notice with at least two months' warning. Tenants can ask a tribunal to check it's in line with the market.
- No bidding wars. Landlords and agents must advertise a clear rent and can't ask for or accept offers above it.
- Rent in advance is limited. You can't ask for rent before the tenancy agreement is signed, and no more than one month's rent upfront once it is.
- Fair treatment. It's now unlawful to refuse tenants because they have children or receive benefits. Every applicant should be judged on their own circumstances.
- Pets. Tenants can ask to keep a pet. You must reply within 28 days and can only refuse for a good reason, such as a lease that bans pets.
- Written terms. Every tenant must have the main terms of their tenancy in writing.

#### What's still to come

15 December 2026The new landlord database opens, starting with the West Midlands and rolling out region by region.

15 August to 14 November 2027Registration window for landlords in the South West, including Somerset. The fee is £65 per property each year.

Expected 2028A new Private Rented Sector Ombudsman. All landlords will have to join, so tenants have somewhere to take complaints.

By 2030Planned minimum energy rating of EPC C for rented homes, with a cap on what you must spend.

2035 onwards (proposed)The Decent Homes Standard extended to private rented homes, along with firm deadlines for fixing damp, mould and other hazards ("Awaab's Law").

Good news for good landlords. If your property is safe, fairly priced and well looked after, very little changes day to day. Most tenants want to stay put, and the new rules reward landlords who keep them happy.

Dates for later stages come from government announcements as of October 2026 and may change. We'll keep you updated.

Finding the right tenant
Marketing and referencing

### Finding the right tenant

Now that tenancies are open-ended, choosing the right tenant is more important than ever. We'd always rather take a few extra days to find someone who'll look after your home and stay for years.

#### Marketing your property

We'll write a clear, honest description, take good photographs and advertise your property on our website and the main property portals confirm which portals. We also contact people already registered with us who are looking for a home like yours.

#### Viewings

We arrange and attend every viewing, so you don't need to be there. We'll show the property at its best, answer questions and give you honest feedback afterwards. If tenants are still living there, we'll agree viewing times with them in advance.

#### Choosing between applicants

The law now sets clear rules for this stage. Every applicant must be considered fairly, without blanket bans on families with children or people receiving benefits. We'll talk you through each applicant's circumstances and help you make a sound, lawful decision.

#### Holding deposit

Once you accept an applicant, they can pay a holding deposit of up to one week's rent while references are checked. It's normally put towards their first month's rent.

#### Our referencing

Before anyone moves in, we carry out thorough checks on every adult tenant and any guarantor:

- Identity and Right to Rent
- Income and affordability
- Employment or other income evidence
- Credit history
- Previous landlord reference
- Guarantor checks where needed

We share the results with you before anything is signed. Confirm referencing provider

Moving in
Starting the tenancy

### Moving in day

A well-organised start sets the tone for the whole tenancy. Here's what happens between saying yes to a tenant and handing over the keys.

- The tenancy agreement. We prepare a written agreement that complies with the new rules and sets out the rent, what's included and who is responsible for what. Everyone signs it before the tenancy begins.
- First payment. The tenant pays the deposit and no more than one month's rent in advance. We hold these funds until the tenancy starts.
- Deposit protection. We register the deposit with name of deposit scheme within 30 days and give the tenant the required information about how it's protected.
- Inventory and check-in. A detailed inventory with photographs records the condition of the property and its contents on the day. The tenant checks and signs it. This is your best protection if there's a dispute at the end.
- Safety checks on the day. We test the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and record that they work.
- Documents for the tenant. We give the tenant copies of the gas safety certificate, electrical report, EPC and deposit information, and keep a record that they've been received.
- Meters and bills. We take meter readings and let the utility companies and Somerset Council (for council tax) know who is responsible from the start date.
- Keys. The tenant collects their keys, and we keep a set for inspections and emergencies.

##### Keep good records

Many disputes come down to what can be proved. We keep signed copies of every document, certificate and inventory on file for the life of the tenancy and beyond.

During the tenancy
Managing your let

### During the tenancy

On our fully managed service, this is where we earn our fee. Our aim is a home that stays in good condition, rent that arrives on time and tenants who want to stay.

#### Rent and statements

We collect the rent each month and pay it into your account, less our fees, within X working days, with a clear statement showing every payment and cost. Client money is held in a separate client account and protected by client money protection scheme.

#### If the rent is late

We act quickly and politely. Most late payments are sorted with a phone call. If arrears build up, we'll talk to you about the options, which may include serving a Section 8 notice. We can also tell you about rent guarantee products that cover lost rent confirm wording.

#### Property inspections

We visit to check the property is being looked after and to spot maintenance issues early, e.g. first visit after three months, then every six months. You'll receive a written report with photos. Tenants must be given at least 24 hours' written notice of a visit.

#### Rent reviews

We keep an eye on the local market and recommend a fair increase when it's due. Under the new rules the rent can go up once a year using a Section 13 notice with two months' warning. A sensible, market-level rise rarely gets challenged.

#### Repairs and maintenance

Tenants report problems to us, and we arrange trusted local contractors to put things right. We'll always check with you before spending above an agreed limit, except in a genuine emergency. Our 24-hour repair support means tenants have someone to call if the boiler fails on a winter night confirm out-of-hours arrangements.

##### Damp and mould

Damp and mould is one of the most common problems in rented homes and is taken very seriously by councils. We look for it at every inspection, investigate the cause when it's reported, and recommend a lasting fix rather than a coat of paint.

#### Pets

Tenants can now ask to keep a pet, and you must respond within 28 days. We'll help you consider each request fairly and agree sensible conditions.

#### Keeping certificates up to date

We track the renewal date for every certificate and arrange renewals in good time, so your property stays compliant without you having to remember.

Ending a tenancy
Ending a tenancy

### When a tenancy ends

Most tenancies end because the tenant decides to move on. When you need the property back, the law now requires a clear reason and the correct notice. We'll guide you through it.

#### When your tenant leaves

Tenants can end the tenancy at any time with two months' written notice. We'll arrange a check-out, re-advertise the property straight away if you'd like to re-let, and keep the gap between tenants as short as possible.

#### Check-out and the deposit

At check-out we compare the property against the inventory, allowing for fair wear and tear. Where there's damage or cleaning needed, we agree deductions with you and the tenant. If they can't be agreed, the deposit scheme's free dispute service decides, based on the evidence. This is where a good inventory really pays off.

#### When you need the property back

Section 21 "no-fault" notices no longer exist. Instead, you serve a Section 8 notice on the official form, stating the legal ground you're relying on. If the tenant doesn't leave, you apply to the court for possession.

Using a ground you don't genuinely intend to rely on can lead to a fine of up to £40,000. Always talk to us before serving a notice.

#### The most common grounds

Reason | Notice | Points to know

Selling the property | 4 months | Not in the first 12 months of a tenancy. You can't re-let the property for 12 months afterwards.

You or a close family member moving in | 4 months | Not in the first 12 months. The same 12-month restriction on re-letting applies.

Serious rent arrears | 4 weeks | At least three months' rent owed when the notice is served and at the court hearing. The court must give possession.

Some arrears, or persistent late payment | 4 weeks | The court decides whether possession is reasonable.

Breaking the tenancy terms | 2 weeks | For example, damage or unauthorised occupants. The court decides.

Anti-social behaviour | Immediate | Serious cases can go straight to court once the notice is served.

A notice can be used to start court proceedings for up to 12 months. For most grounds, the court won't grant possession if the deposit wasn't protected properly. This table is a summary, not legal advice.

Your checklist
At a glance

### Your landlord checklist

Tick these off before your tenancy starts. If you're fully managed, we'll take care of most of them for you.

##### Before marketing

- Mortgage lender consent, if needed
- Freeholder or lease permission, if leasehold
- Landlord insurance in place
- Valid EPC, rated E or above
- Gas safety certificate
- Electrical safety report (EICR)
- Smoke and CO alarms fitted where required
- Legionella risk assessment
- HMO or other licence, if required
- Property clean, repaired and presentable

##### Before the tenant moves in

- References and Right to Rent checks complete
- Tenancy agreement signed
- Deposit received and protected within 30 days
- Inventory and check-in completed
- Alarms tested on the first day
- Tenant given all certificates and deposit information
- Meter readings taken, utilities and council tax updated

##### Coming up

- Register on the landlord database when the South West window opens (15 August to 14 November 2027)
- Plan any energy improvements ahead of the EPC C target
- Join the landlord ombudsman when it launches

#### Tax and your rental income

Rental profits are taxable, and you'll usually need to report them to HMRC each year. Making Tax Digital for Income Tax now applies to landlords and sole traders with qualifying income over £50,000, and the threshold falls to £30,000 from April 2027 and £20,000 from April 2028. If you live abroad, special rules apply to how your rent is paid.

We'd always recommend speaking to an accountant about your own position. We can provide annual statements to make their job easier.

## Renting your next home,
made simple.

A plain-English guide to renting with us in Taunton and the Quantocks: finding a home, moving in, your rights in 2026, and what happens when you move on.

Updated for the Renters' Rights Act

Welcome
Welcome

### A home, not just a let

Moving home is a big step. This guide explains what to expect at every stage of renting with Quantock Lettings, what you'll need to do, and the rights you have as a tenant in 2026.

We're a small, local team in Taunton. We look after homes across Taunton, Bridgwater, Wellington, Bishops Lydeard and the Quantock villages, and we'd like you to feel settled and looked after in yours.

We believe renting works best when everyone knows where they stand. We'll be clear about costs from the start, fix problems properly when you report them, and treat you fairly and with respect throughout your tenancy.

The law on renting changed on 1 May 2026, giving tenants more security and more say. We've explained the main changes in plain English on page 6. If anything isn't clear, just ask us.

Neil, Cheryl and Hattie

Finding your home
Searching and viewing

### Finding your home

Good homes in our area often let quickly, so it pays to be ready. Here's how to give yourself the best chance.

#### Start your search

You'll find our available homes on our website, quantocklettings.co.uk, and on the major property portals. Tell us what you're looking for and we'll let you know when something suitable comes up, often before it's advertised.

#### Before you view

- Work out what you can comfortably afford each month, including bills and council tax.
- Think about who will live with you, any pets, and when you'd like to move.
- Have your ID and proof of income ready, so you can apply straight away if you find the right home.

#### At the viewing

We'll show you round and answer your questions. Take your time, open cupboards, check the heating and look at the garden. If tenants still live there, please respect their home.

Fair renting rules. Since 1 May 2026, every home must be advertised at a clear rent, and nobody can ask you to bid above it. Landlords and agents can't refuse you just because you have children or receive benefits.

##### Questions worth asking

- What's included: white goods, carpets, curtains?
- How is the home heated, and what's the EPC rating?
- What's the council tax band?
- Is there parking, and is the broadband good?
- Are pets considered? (You can always ask.)
- When is the home available?
- Who should I call if something goes wrong?

Applying
Applying and referencing

### Applying for a home

Found the one? Here's what happens next, and exactly what you can and can't be asked to pay.

#### Holding deposit

To take a home off the market while we check references, you may be asked for a holding deposit of up to one week's rent. It's usually put towards your first month's rent.

You'll get it back within 7 days if the landlord decides not to go ahead. It can only be kept if you give false or misleading information, fail a Right to Rent check, pull out yourself, or don't take reasonable steps to complete the tenancy within the agreed deadline (normally 15 days).

#### Referencing

We check every adult who will live in the home. Be ready to provide:

- Photo ID and proof of your right to rent in the UK
- Proof of income, such as payslips or bank statements
- Details of your employer or other income
- Your current or previous landlord's contact details
- Permission for a credit check

If your income doesn't quite cover the rent, a guarantor can help. They agree to pay if you can't, and we'll reference them too. Referencing is free for you.

#### What you may be asked to pay

The law limits what tenants can be charged. You can only be asked for:

Payment | Limit

Rent in advance | No more than one month, and only after you've signed

Holding deposit | Up to one week's rent

Tenancy deposit | Up to five weeks' rent (six if the annual rent is £50,000 or more)

Changes you ask for to your tenancy | Up to £50, or reasonable costs if higher

Lost keys or security devices | The reasonable cost of replacing them

Rent paid more than 14 days late | Interest of up to 3% above the Bank of England base rate

Bills | Utilities, council tax, TV licence and broadband, if your agreement says you pay them

We never charge for viewings, referencing, tenancy paperwork or check-in.

Moving in
Starting your tenancy

### Moving in

We want moving day to be straightforward. Here's what happens, and what to do in your first few days.

- Sign your tenancy agreement. We'll send you a written agreement setting out the rent, the payment date, what's included and who looks after what. Read it carefully and ask us about anything you're unsure of.
- Pay your deposit and first month's rent. Your holding deposit is usually taken off the first payment.
- Your deposit is protected. We register it in a government-approved scheme within 30 days and send you details of how it's protected and how to get it back.
- Check the inventory. You'll get a detailed record of the home's condition, with photos. Check it carefully and tell us within the agreed time if anything is missing or wrong. This protects you when you move out.
- Collect your keys. On moving day we'll hand over the keys, show you the meters, stopcock and boiler, and check the smoke and carbon monoxide alarms are working.
- Keep your documents. You'll receive the gas safety certificate, electrical safety report, Energy Performance Certificate and deposit information. Keep them somewhere safe.

##### In your first week

- Take meter readings and photos of them
- Set up your gas, electricity and water accounts
- Register for council tax with Somerset Council
- Arrange broadband and a TV licence if you need one
- Take out contents insurance for your belongings
- Set up a standing order for your rent
- Find the stopcock, fuse box and boiler controls

Your rights
Renting in 2026

### Your rights as a tenant

The Renters' Rights Act came into force on 1 May 2026 and covers every private tenancy in England, including ones that started before then. Here's what it means for you.

- No fixed terms. Your tenancy rolls on from month to month. You can stay as long as you keep to your agreement, and leave whenever you like with two months' notice.
- No "no-fault" evictions. Section 21 has gone. A landlord can only ask you to leave for a reason the law allows, such as selling the home, moving in themselves, or serious rent arrears. They must give you the correct written notice, and for selling or moving in that's four months.
- A settled first year. Your landlord can't use the selling or moving-in reasons during the first 12 months of your tenancy.
- Fair rent increases. Rent can go up only once a year, with at least two months' written notice on the official form. If you think a rise is above the going rate, you can ask the First-tier Tribunal to decide.
- Pets. You can ask to keep a pet. Your landlord must reply within 28 days and can only refuse for a good reason.
- Fair treatment. No one can refuse you a home because you have children or receive benefits.
- A safe home. Your landlord must keep the home safe and in good repair, including the structure, heating, hot water and any gas and electrics, and deal with serious damp and mould.
- Your deposit is safe. It must be protected in a government-approved scheme, and there's a free service to settle any disagreement at the end.

Coming soon. A national register of landlords opens from December 2026, and a Private Rented Sector Ombudsman is expected in 2028.

#### If your landlord needs the home back

Reason | Minimum notice | Good to know

Landlord selling, or moving in themselves or family | 4 months | Can't be used in your first 12 months

Serious rent arrears | 4 weeks | At least three months' rent owed

Breaking the tenancy terms | 2 weeks | A court decides whether it's reasonable

You don't have to leave until a court orders it. This is a summary of the law in England as of October 2026, not legal advice. Shelter and Citizens Advice offer free, independent help.

Living in your home
During your tenancy

### Living in your home

Most tenancies run smoothly with a little give and take. Here's how things work day to day.

#### Paying your rent

Your rent is due on the date in your tenancy agreement. A standing order is the easiest way to make sure it always arrives on time. If you're struggling to pay, please tell us early. It's far easier to find a way forward before arrears build up.

#### Reporting repairs

Tell us about any repair as soon as you notice it, using the Report maintenance form on our website, by phone or by email. Photos help us send the right contractor first time. We'll let you know when someone will visit.

#### Inspections

We visit from time to time to check the home is in good order and to spot any repairs needed. We'll always give you at least 24 hours' written notice, except in a genuine emergency.

#### Changes in your circumstances

Let us know if someone wants to move in or out, if you're going away for a long period, or if your contact details change.

##### Emergencies: call us straight away

For a gas leak, flooding, no heating or hot water in cold weather, an electrical fault that's dangerous, or a home that isn't secure, call 01823 765654.

If you smell gas, leave the home and call the National Gas Emergency Service on 0800 111 999 first. For a power cut, call 105.

#### Damp and mould

Everyday life puts a lot of moisture into the air. You can help keep your home healthy:

- Use extractor fans when cooking and showering
- Open windows for a while each day, even in winter
- Dry washing outside or in a well-ventilated room
- Keep furniture slightly away from outside walls
- Wipe away condensation from windows each morning

If you see damp or mould, please report it straight away. We'll find the cause and put it right.

Looking after your home
Your part

### Looking after your home

Your landlord looks after the building and its main systems. Day-to-day care is down to you, and a well-kept home makes getting your deposit back simple.

#### Everyday care

- Keep the home clean and aired
- Test the smoke alarms monthly and replace batteries if needed
- Keep the garden tidy, lawns cut and paths clear
- Put bins out on the right day
- Replace light bulbs and keep drains and sinks clear
- Keep the home heated in winter to stop pipes freezing
- Lock up and close windows when you go out

#### Going away

If you'll be away for more than a couple of weeks, especially in winter, let us know. Leave the heating on low and tell us who holds a spare key.

#### Please ask us first

Some changes need your landlord's written permission. Please check with us before you:

- Decorate, put up shelves or change fixtures
- Let someone else move in, or sublet
- Keep a pet
- Change the locks
- Run a business from the home
- Fit a satellite dish or make alterations

We'll pass your request to the landlord and come back to you promptly. Pet requests must be answered within 28 days.

Moving out
Ending your tenancy

### Moving out

When it's time to move on, a little planning makes it smooth and helps you get your full deposit back.

#### Giving notice

You can end your tenancy at any time by giving at least two months' notice in writing. Email is fine. If you're renting with others, talk to them first, as notice from one tenant usually ends the tenancy for everyone.

#### Check-out

We'll arrange a time to check the home against your inventory, allowing for fair wear and tear. Please hand back every key, including spares.

#### Getting your deposit back

If there are no deductions, we'll arrange for your deposit to be returned promptly. If we think something needs deducting, such as cleaning or damage beyond fair wear and tear, we'll explain why and show you the evidence. Once the amount is agreed, it must be paid within 10 days.

If you don't agree, the deposit scheme offers a free, independent dispute service that looks at the evidence from both sides.

##### Moving-out checklist

- Give two months' written notice
- Clean thoroughly, including the oven, fridge and windows
- Remove all your belongings and rubbish
- Cut the lawn and tidy the garden
- Repair any damage you've caused, or tell us about it
- Take final meter readings and photos
- Tell your energy, water and broadband suppliers
- Tell Somerset Council about your council tax
- Redirect your post
- Give us your forwarding address
- Return every key

Tip: compare the home with your check-in inventory and photos before you leave. It's the quickest way to spot anything that needs doing.

At a glance

### Checklist and useful contacts

Keep this page handy. It has everything you need in one place.

##### Ready to apply

- Photo ID for every adult who'll live there
- Proof of your right to rent
- Three months of payslips or bank statements
- Employer and previous landlord contact details
- Guarantor details, if you need one

##### Before you move in

- Tenancy agreement read and signed
- Deposit and first month's rent paid
- Deposit protection details received
- Gas, electrical and EPC certificates received
- Inventory checked and returned
- Contents insurance arranged
